summary:
Kansas Senate Bill 244 was enacted on 26 February 2026 when the Legislature overrode Governor Laura Kelly's veto, and it took effect immediately. The law confines transgender people to sex-segregated facilities matching sex assigned at birth in publicly owned buildings, a category the Human Rights Campaign records as covering schools, universities, airports and government offices. It creates civil and criminal penalties of up to $1,000 for using a non-matching facility and authorises bounty-style lawsuits of at least $1,000 by any private person who claims to have shared a bathroom with a transgender person.

The same law bars the updating of driver's licences and state identification cards and invalidates existing licences whose gender marker is inconsistent with sex assigned at birth. The Kansas Department of Revenue has been mailing written notice, and many holders have already been told their licence is now invalid. Reissue is at the holder's expense with no grace period, and surrender letters warn of additional penalties for driving without a valid credential.

Two transgender men filed Doe v. State of Kansas in Douglas County District Court within days of enactment, represented by the ACLU and Ballard Spahr, citing fear of violence under the facility-restriction and identification-invalidation provisions.

The identification rules rest on an earlier statute. Senate Bill 180 was enacted in April 2023 by veto override, defined biological sex in state law and barred agencies from recognising genders beyond sex assigned at birth. The attorney general then directed that new or updated driver's licences and birth certificates reflect only original sex at birth. A temporary restraining order barred gender-marker changes; the Kansas Court of Appeals reversed unanimously on 13 June 2025 for lack of evidence of irreparable harm to law-enforcement identification; and in October 2025 the Kansas Supreme Court rejected an appeal, allowing the Department of Revenue to continue the changes.

Kansas law has prohibited discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations since 2020, following Bostock v. Clayton County and Kansas Human Rights Commission action in August 2020 covering businesses with four or more employees. The state hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by sexual orientation but does not cover gender identity; federal law has covered both since October 2009.

Marriage for same-sex couples became available after U.S. District Judge Daniel D. Crabtree ruled the state ban unconstitutional on 4 November 2014, effective 12 November 2014, and became fully legal under Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015, with all judicial districts issuing licences by the end of that month. Consensual same-sex sexual activity is legal under Lawrence v. Texas (2003), which rendered Kansas's sodomy law unenforceable, though the Legislature has not repealed its same-sex-only sodomy provisions carrying historic penalties of six months in jail and/or $1,000.
tangentialFactors:
A trans-focused legal-risk assessment published on 20 February 2026 moved Kansas from its "Worst Laws" tier to "Do Not Travel," the first state added to that tier in a year, citing the bathroom-bounty law that lets private individuals sue transgender people encountered in wrong-sex facilities. The assessment addresses exposure during interstate travel, meaning a visitor whose route passes through Kansas faces the same facility and identification rules as a resident.

The bounty provision is the operative enforcement mechanism: it does not depend on a state agency or prosecutor initiating action, since any private person can sue. That changes the practical exposure for a visitor using a public building, including an airport, during a trip.
localsOnly:
Kansas banned transgender athletes from female school sports teams through a veto override in March 2023, effective 1 July 2023, after earlier bans passed in April 2021 and April 2022 were vetoed twice. The Kansas State High School Activities Association as of February 2023 left decisions case-by-case to schools.

Gender-affirming care for minors under 18 is banned. Governor Kelly vetoed Senate Bill 233 on 12 April 2024 and the override failed by two votes; she vetoed similar Senate Bill 63 in February 2025 and that override succeeded on 18 February 2025. In May 2026 State District Judge Carl Folsom III granted a temporary injunction blocking enforcement in an ACLU-backed parental lawsuit.

Three municipalities banned conversion therapy on minors: Roeland Park in June 2020, Lawrence in April 2021 and Prairie Village in October 2021. In 2022 a Geary County middle-school teacher obtained a partial federal preliminary injunction allowing her to use students' non-preferred names and to disclose students' gender identity to parents despite a school preferred-name requirement.

Married same-sex couples may adopt. Lesbian couples may access in vitro fertilisation, with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognised only if married. The state permits gestational and traditional surrogacy on equal terms for same-sex and different-sex couples, but adoption agencies may refuse placements that violate their religious or moral convictions, and under In the Matter of Adoption of I.M. (November 2012) and Frazier v. Goudschaal (22 February 2013) unmarried non-biological partners obtain rights only in limited best-interest circumstances.

Sexual-orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations has been prohibited since 2020 under Bostock and Kansas Human Rights Commission enforcement, supplemented by city ordinances and executive orders issued in 2007, rescinded in 2015 and reissued in 2019. Voters in Salina and Hutchinson repealed local ordinances on 6 November 2012. In March 2024 the Legislature passed a law defining content containing "acts of homosexuality" as harmful to minors alongside pornography and requiring government ID-based age verification to access such material.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of Doe v. State of Kansas is unresolved; the suit was filed within days of SB 244's enactment and no ruling is recorded in the sources.

Enforcement data for SB 244's facility and identification provisions is not sourced. The number of licence holders who have received invalidation notices, and the number of bounty suits filed, are not recorded.

The state hate-crime law's exclusion of gender identity is a statutory gap; whether Kansas prosecutors charge such offences under federal law is not documented in the sources.
